text.p: Here are highlights from Polish newspapers this morning.
RZECZPOSPOLITA

- A 22,900 deadweight tonne (DWT) container ship contracted by a Cypriot shipowner was the last vessel launched this year by the Szczecin shipyard. In 1996 the yard launched 18 vessels earning $500 million, the mangement said.

- The Business Centre Club (BCC), Poland's biggest employers' lobby, urged President Aleksander Kwasniewski not to sign a bill on the tax office's right to check bank accounts. No standard bank account control procedure applies throughout OECD countries and some countries' regulations are more liberal than others', BCC argued.

- Telecommunications, chemicals and raw material processing for the textile industry were Poland's most profitable lines of business in 1996, while arms manufacturing, electronic production and land adaptation works for construction brought the greatest losses, a report by the Banking Education and Research Foundation said.

- Within up to five years, prices of rented office space will start to fall in Warsaw, which is now causing investors to press constructors for time to negotiate the best possible renting contracts, the Austrian Porr construction firm said.
- The Lublin-based Lubelskie Kopalnie Surowcow Mineralnych (LKSM) sand and gravel mines will be privatised next year and the management is now selecting the best privatisation method, LKSM said.
- A banking consortium has supplied the Grajewo chipboard plant with a 106 million zlotys credit to finance modernisation works which will double Grajewo's output by the end of 1998.
- Poland's National Investment Fund (NFI)- Fortuna has sold a 33 percent stake in the Nowiny cement plant to Germany's Dyckerhoff AG cement concern, the NFI Fortuna said.
NOWA EUROPA

- Poland's gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate will remain around five percent next year, whether or not Solidarity wins parliamentary elections, the Swiss UBS bank said. UBS expressed support for strict monetarist policies by the National Bank of Poland (NBP), the central bank.

- The Suwalki Special Economic Zone (SEZ) president Jerzy Malysz and the deputy president Andrzej Soroka have resigned as the result of criticism by prime minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz of family links within the SEZ company management.
- The Gdanski Stocznia Polnocna shipyard has received an International Standards Organisation (ISO)-9001 quality certificate awarded by Germanischer Lloyd and the Polish Shipping Register.
- Poland's domestic demand will remain strong until the end of December, a report by NICOM Consulting said.

- Bank Handlowy's Capital Operations Centre (BH COK), in a report dated November 22, recommended buying Bank Inicjatyw Gospodarczych (BIG) shares due to low operational costs and the bank's improved fianancial results.

- Credit Suisse Investment Management (CSIM) is one of the first financial institutions to manage portfolios through a contracted securities house. CSIM will not operate its own brokerage in Poland, its president Jonathan S. Woollet said.
GAZETA WYBORCZA

- The Fiat plant in Bielsko Biala, southern Poland, will start assemblying a test series of the Fiat Siena model after the New Year. The new model will appear on sale in the second half of 1997, Fiat said.
- The Warsaw-based Ursus plant's annual net loss will reach 35 million zlotys this year but the tractor maker expects profits in 1997, its director general Janusz Sciskalski said.

- Poland's National Investment Funds have sold a 60 percent stake in the Radom-based Radomskie Zaklady Garbarskie RZG tannery plant to the Centrum Skory (CS) firm. CS will invest three million zlotys in the plant's sewage treatment facility which is the main condition of the tannery's operation.
ZYCIE

- The state-owned PKP railway company will contract 50 technologically-advanced engines worth $210 million from the Wroclaw-based Pafawag plant today. The purchase was a condition for Pafawag's takeover by the Adtranz engine maker.
-- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
